76ae4665bb5aad90: FOR all the talk of conferences, exhibitions and corporate meetings, some of the most important business can happen away from the ballroom.
Maybe it's a conversation over dinner, or an introduction made during a coffee break.
It could even be during an informal exchange between delegates who might otherwise never have crossed paths.
That's part of the reason why face-to-face business events continue to matter, even as companies become increasingly comfortable with virtual meetings and digital communication.
And it's also helping to shape Malaysia's growing role as a destination for international business events.

The country's meetings, incentives, conferences and exhibitions (MICE) sector had a strong 2025, with the Malaysia Convention and Exhibition Bureau (MyCEB) reporting 393 business events and an estimated RM4.07 billion in economic impact from international delegates.

The momentum has continued into 2026. As of June 30, MyCEB had secured 416 international business events scheduled to take place between 2026 and 2030, with a projected economic impact of RM3.98 billion.

For Malaysia, the attraction is fairly straightforward. Its location puts it within relatively easy reach of major markets across Southeast Asia and the wider Asia-Pacific, while its established air links, transport networks, hotels and convention facilities make it a practical choice for organisers.

Cost also plays a part. Compared with some of the region's more expensive business destinations, Malaysia offers a combination of convention facilities, accommodation, food and transport at a relatively competitive price point.
For those working on the ground, however, the considerations go beyond simply finding a venue large enough to accommodate a crowd.

Sarah Yap, sales manager and head of tours at YES Travel and Holidays (YES Travel), which has more than 16 years of experience organising incentive trips and corporate programmes, says companies are becoming more purposeful about what they want their employees to gain from travelling together.
The emphasis, she observes, is increasingly on creating experiences that strengthen teams, recognise performance and give people an opportunity to connect outside the workplace.
BEYOND THE CONFERENCE ROOM
The value of business events increasingly lies in what happens around the formal programme.
A three-day conference can bring together researchers, investors, corporate leaders and industry specialists from different countries.
An incentive trip can allow employees to reconnect outside the workplace.
An exhibition can put potential business partners in the same space and allow conversations to develop in ways that are difficult to replicate online.
Those interactions can have an economic ripple effect well beyond hotels and airlines.
Restaurants, transport operators, event companies, technology providers, retailers and professional-services firms can all benefit from the arrival of international delegates.
More significantly, business events can create opportunities for investment, knowledge exchange and commercial partnerships that may continue long after delegates have gone home.
That wider economic contribution is one reason governments and destinations around the world have been competing for a larger share of the business-events market.
For Malaysia, it's a particularly relevant opportunity as the country seeks to attract higher-value international visitors and strengthen its position as a regional business hub.
THE HUMAN CONNECTION
Technology may have made it easier to attend a meeting from thousands of kilometres away, but it hasn't eliminated the value of being in the same room. The emphasis, however, has shifted.
Companies are becoming more deliberate about why they bring people together, rather than organising events simply because an annual meeting or conference appears on the calendar.
Leadership alignment, employee recognition, team building, client relationships and collaboration are increasingly part of the equation.

Yap says this is reflected in the programmes being requested by corporate clients, with greater attention being paid to the experience itself rather than simply ticking off a destination or itinerary.
Incentive travel, in particular, can serve a dual purpose: recognising performance while allowing employees to experience a destination together.
And sometimes the most useful part of a business trip is the part that was never scheduled.
A conversation over a meal can be less formal than a presentation, while a chance meeting at an exhibition can lead to a new contact.
A shared experience too can create a sense of connection that's harder to achieve through a screen.
These are difficult outcomes to quantify, but they're increasingly part of how companies assess the value of bringing people together.
WHAT'S NEXT?
Malaysia's challenge now isn't simply to attract more events, but to ensure the experience keeps pace with what organisers and delegates expect.
Service standards, sustainability, digital technology and the quality of the overall visitor experience are becoming increasingly important considerations.
Infrastructure and venues remain fundamental, but so are the people delivering the experience - from event professionals and hotel staff to transport operators and destination-management companies.
The country's growing pipeline suggests there's confidence in its ability to compete for international business events.

The latest MyCEB figures indicate that the sector isn't merely recovering from the disruption of the pandemic; it's increasingly being positioned as an important part of Malaysia's wider tourism and economic strategy.

For travellers, this may be a less visible side of tourism. Business delegates don't necessarily arrive with the same itinerary as holidaymakers, yet they contribute to the same ecosystem - filling hotel rooms, eating in restaurants, using transport and, increasingly, adding leisure time to business trips.
That last point is worth watching, too. As business and leisure travel increasingly overlap, a delegate
arriving for a conference may stay on for a few extra days, bring family members along or return later for a holiday after discovering a destination through work.
And that may be the bigger story. A business event is rarely just about what happens on stage.
Increasingly, it's about the people who meet because they happened to be there - and what happens after they return home.

1b1c6884d17908a1: KATHMANDU: Nepali rescuers faced challenging conditions on Sunday as search operations after catastrophic floods entered a 12th day, buoyed by the extraordinary rescues of four survivors.
The glacial and mountain collapse on the China-Nepal border killed at least 1,385 people and left more than 5,500 missing across the two countries.
Rescuers found two more people alive on Saturday, joining two saved the day before in what have been described as miraculous tales of survival.
Three of those have been found in hydropower tunnels where the government initially said it believed more than 100 workers could be alive.
"Search and rescue is going on at the tunnels despite geography, adverse weather and lack of connectivity," Energy Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha told AFP.
Rescue workers were experiencing "multiple challenges", he said.
The wall of icy water and debris tore through mountain districts on August 26, destroying roads, bridges and other infrastructure.
The United Nations chief in Nepal issued an emotional plea for aid, saying survivors of the catastrophic flooding had seen their lives transformed in just "one to two minutes."
"You lose your home, you lose your livelihood, you lose your loved one and you lose the breadwinner of your family," UN Resident Coordinator Lila Pieters Yahia told AFP in Kathmandu on Sunday.
On Saturday, rescuers pulled a Chinese man alive from deep inside a hydropower tunnel, and a 64-year-old Nepali woman, Chandrika Shrestha, from her mud-covered home.
Prime Minister Balendra Shah said Shrestha's rescue had "given hope to the entire nation."
A day earlier, two Nepali hydropower workers were rescued at the Trishuli 3A tunnel, where searches continue alongside multiple other sites, with at least 12 hydropower projects affected.

Other examples of remarkable fortitude have emerged from Nepal, including Rajendra Dawadi, a school principal who quickly ordered an evacuation as the torrent approached, saving hundreds of students' lives.
"If the information was wrong, we would lose a day of schooling," he told AFP.
"But if it was true, we were going to lose our lives."
- DEATH TOLLS RISE -
Biraj Bhakta Shrestha, the energy minister, said work was continuing to restore electricity in several areas.
"Places that have been unreachable, we've tried to restore power with solar," he told AFP.
Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal has called the disaster a "Himalayan tsunami" and warned reconstruction costs could run into the billions of dollars.
The UN has said the magnitude of the destruction makes delivering aid an immense challenge. It launched a US$50 million appeal to help more than 84,000 people.
With mortuaries overflowing, Nepal has buried hundreds of bodies in mass graves, after taking DNA samples for future identification, according to the police.
Only around 100 bodies have been identified and handed over to families.
Nepal will hold a national day of mourning on Monday, the 13th day since the disaster, in line with a traditional period of mourning in Hindu rituals.
While the exact cause of the glacial collapse is unclear, climate change is accelerating glacial melting worldwide, increasing the risk of such disasters.
In Nepal, rescuers have retrieved 1,342 bodies, while around 4,996 people remain missing, according to the disaster agency.
The death toll from the disaster in Tibet has risen from 31 to 43, Chinese state news agency Xinhua reported on Sunday.
A further 519 people are missing, it said.
Foreign journalists cannot travel freely in China's Tibet Autonomous Region and may only visit as part of strictly controlled trips organised by the authorities.
Chinese media have primarily focused their reporting on the scale of search and rescue operations, and have not broadcast footage showing the reactions of families.
The combined toll is 1,385 dead and more than 5,500 missing, including around 800 foreigners, among them tourists and pilgrims.--AFP

47c83e7b5cc56959: BETRAWATI: Believing she had perished in Nepal's deadly floods, the family of Chandika Kumari Shrestha started the ritual of mourning the elderly woman's death.
Ten days later, rescuers found her alive inside her collapsed home in the devastated Betrawati village, where she had survived in a narrow pocket of air amid water and mud.
"The four-storey house was swept (away) by the floods and the house was left in the middle of a quicksand. While walking around it, we heard a voice 'save me,'" police officer Mahendra Darnal said.
In a rescue operation on Saturday lasting 45 minutes, Darnal and his team found Shrestha in a confined space and sent her to an army hospital.
"I was in touch with the family and they had started the 11-day mourning period," Darnal said.

Shrestha was among the hundreds missing in Betrawati, an area among the hardest hit by the floods in Nepal and engulfed with white deposits compacted almost like concrete. Crews continue to recover scores of dead bodies.

The town's market and most residential buildings, some as tall as four storeys, were almost completely buried under debris left by a torrent that swept through the valley, part of a disaster that killed more than 1,300 people across Nepal. Thousands remain unaccounted for.

Rescue workers wearing hard hats were seen digging with shovels, while some were crawling through the gaps of collapsed buildings periodically blowing whistles to get the attention of anyone trapped and alive.
Five days earlier, 24 bodies were found in a decomposed state in Betrawati's market area in a building that had contained a small shop, Darnal said.
Eleven days since a glacial collapse triggered the devastating floods, close to 5,000 are still missing.

Hundreds of bodies have been swept onto the banks of rivers far from the ravaged Rasuwa district. In Chitwan, hundreds of miles away, several rounds of mass burials have taken place for unidentified and badly decomposed bodies.
Even as hope is beginning to fade, Nepal authorities continue their effort to look for people stuck in tunnels and under the thick deposits of mud that have hardened over buildings.
Since Friday, they have pulled out three people from the tunnels, including a Chinese citizen by the Trishuli river, where more than 900 are believed to be trapped.
Others like Shrestha have survived in extraordinary conditions, including an 8-year-old boy who was also reunited with his mother.--REUTERS
c19290b34c561222: LONDON: Britain's finance minister, John Healey, will use his first major speech since taking office seven weeks ago to set out how prime minister Andy Burnham's plan to devolve power away from central government can help revive growth across the country.

In a speech at a manufacturing site on Monday, Healey is expected to announce plans to give city regions greater powers to develop local industrial strategies and attract private investment, as part of a push to bring growth to "every postcode".

"I want to see wealth creation in this country. I want to see businesses make a profit. And to create the conditions for that we need an active, accountable state at all levels to remove blockages and create the conditions for more investment," Healey is expected to say, according to a release from his office.
He will also use the speech to stress his commitment to "fiscal discipline" as he pursues faster growth in Britain's sluggish economy.

The challenges have been mounting for Healey ahead of his debut budget on Oct 28, as investors worry about the inflationary impact of rising oil prices from the Iran war, shrinking budget headroom, and rising spending commitments.

Healey will announce that £150 million (US$203 million) of funding already allocated from the British Business Bank will be earmarked for innovative firms in the north of England, pumping in between £5 million and £15 million designed to attract additional private capital.

Healey and Burnham have already pledged to stick to the fiscal rules adopted by the previous government, including a target of balancing day-to-day spending with tax revenues by the end of the decade.
But given Burnham's plans for expanded social care and more defence spending, Healey is already under pressure to raise billions of pounds in tax at the budget.
30c4c0ceed11c56d: IF neighbouring states increasingly function as interconnected economic regions, Malaysia must confront a larger question.
Does the country possess the fiscal and institutional architecture required to govern such an economy?

For decades, debates on Malaysian federalism have understandably concentrated on constitutional authority, grants, petroleum revenues, development allocations and the distribution of responsibilities between the federal government and the states.
These questions remain important. But redistribution is not the same as integration.

A state can receive larger federal transfers yet remain economically disconnected from the rest of the country. Another can attract billions of ringgit in investment while generating weak linkages with Malaysian suppliers.
A third can record high GDP even though the income generated by its productive assets is not proportionately reflected in household welfare.
The next phase of Malaysian federalism must therefore move beyond asking only who receives what.
It must also ask how the Federation produces together.
Three Pillars of Economic Federalism
Malaysia needs to distinguish between three related concepts. Fiscal federalism concerns revenues, expenditure responsibilities and transfers between governments.
Regional planning concerns infrastructure, transport, housing, environmental management and public services whose economic effects frequently cross administrative boundaries.
Production federalism concerns the relationships connecting industries, workers, suppliers, universities, technologies, logistics and investment across states.
Malaysia already practises elements of all three. The problem is that they are insufficiently connected.

Federal budgets may finance infrastructure without systematically measuring the additional production generated across neighbouring states. Investment incentives may attract factories without adequately determining whether Malaysian suppliers become part of their value chains.
State development strategies may compete for similar industries when regional specialisation would generate greater collective value.

An integrated production economy requires all three pillars to reinforce one another. Fiscal federalism finances capability. Regional planning connects geography. Production federalism connects economic activity.
Transfers Cannot Substitute for Productive Capacity
Fiscal transfers remain essential, especially where poorer or geographically disadvantaged states face higher costs in providing roads, schools, healthcare and basic infrastructure.

Indeed, the government's pre-budget statement 2027 explicitly emphasises narrowing regional development gaps while tailoring development strategies to the strengths and potential of individual states and regions.
But transfers alone cannot eliminate structural economic disparities.

Where industrial linkages are weak, investment limited, skills inadequate and connectivity poor, additional public expenditure can improve services without necessarily transforming the productive structure.
Fiscal redistribution addresses differences in resources. Production policy addresses differences in economic capability. Malaysia needs both.
The objective should therefore be not merely to compensate regions for being weaker, but to use fiscal policy to strengthen their capacity to produce, connect and specialise.
This suggests several reforms.

First, intergovernmental transfers should become increasingly transparent and predictable, with clearer consideration of population, fiscal capacity, infrastructure deficits, geography and the differing costs of delivering comparable public services.
Second, Malaysia should consider Regional Development Compacts between the federal government and participating states around agreed economic objectives.
A northern compact could coordinate semiconductors, advanced manufacturing, water, logistics and talent across Penang, Kedah and adjoining areas.
A southern arrangement could coordinate transport, manufacturing, logistics and housing across increasingly interconnected economic corridors.
Sabah and Sarawak would require arrangements reflecting their distinct constitutional positions, geography and development requirements.
Funding could then support agreed regional outcomes rather than merely collections of isolated projects.
Reward Cooperation, Not Duplication
Federal incentives should also encourage states to cooperate where benefits cross borders.
Suppose Penang and Kedah jointly develop technical training serving semiconductor companies in both states. Or Selangor and Negri Sembilan coordinate industrial transport infrastructure.
Or regional logistics investments in Sabah and Sarawak reduce supply-chain costs across multiple jurisdictions.
Projects producing demonstrable cross-border spillovers should qualify for stronger federal support.
The principle is straightforward: Where economic benefits cross state boundaries, fiscal incentives should encourage governments to behave accordingly. This requires better measurement.

Malaysia's national Input-Output tables already show how industries purchase inputs from and supply outputs to one another. But conventional state GDP cannot adequately show how production in one Malaysian region depends upon another.
Regional Input-Output analysis could. How much of Penang's electronics output depends upon Kedah? How much of Sabah's economy purchases inputs from Peninsular Malaysia?

How much of Sarawak's industrial value remains within Sarawak? Which regions possess strong Malaysian backward linkages, and which rely heavily upon imported intermediate inputs? Where are the largest leakages from domestic production chains?
These are not academic questions. They determine whether an investment creates a wider Malaysian multiplier or remains largely an economic enclave.

The Statistics Department already records interregional merchandise trade between Peninsular Malaysia, Sabah and Sarawak. The statistical foundations therefore exist for progressively deeper analysis.
Regional and ultimately interregional Input-Output frameworks should become regular instruments of national development planning.
Institutions That See Beyond State Borders
Data alone, however, cannot solve coordination failures.
Malaysia should consider permanent regional production councils for its major economic corridors.
These should not constitute another layer of government or assume powers belonging constitutionally to federal or state authorities.
They should be coordinating institutions bringing together relevant ministries, state governments, investment agencies, infrastructure providers, universities and industry.
Their purpose would be practical. Is industrial land being developed without sufficient water or electricity? Are universities training workers without reference to emerging regional demand?
Are ports, railways and highways being planned independently? Are neighbouring states using public resources to duplicate essentially identical industrial clusters?
Regional institutions should identify and resolve precisely these failures.
Federalism as Economic Architecture
Federalism is therefore more than a political arrangement governing the distribution of authority. It is also economic architecture.

Malaysia contains markedly different regional economies. The Klang Valley is services-intensive and highly urbanised. Northern Malaysia contains one of Southeast Asia's important electronics and semiconductor concentrations. Johor is expanding around manufacturing, logistics and integration with Singapore. Sabah and Sarawak possess different combinations of resources, geography, infrastructure constraints and development opportunities.
Uniform policy therefore has limits. But complete decentralisation has limits too.
Malaysia requires national coordination precisely because its regional economies are different.
The objective is not uniformity. It is complementarity.
A factory in Kulim should create opportunities for suppliers in Penang and Perak. A data centre in Johor should generate engineering and service demand elsewhere in Malaysia.

Resource development in Sarawak should build Malaysian technological and supplier capabilities. Infrastructure in Sabah should reduce the cost of participating in national as well as international production networks.
The federation becomes economically stronger when value created in one region generates productive opportunities in another.
State confidence creates ambition. Regional cooperation creates scale. Fiscal architecture creates incentives. Production linkages create multipliers. Institutions make the system durable.

Only then does an even harder question arise. What happens when a state appears prosperous in terms of production, but that prosperity is not proportionately reflected in the incomes of its households?
That is where the next discussion should begin: with the Sarawak paradox, and the critical distinction between the geography of production and the geography of welfare.

d65b56277d79c11a: MONZA: Kimi Antonelli had every reason to pinch himself on Sunday after his spectacular triumph for Mercedes from 19th on the grid gave the Monza fans a first home winner of the Italian Grand Prix for 60 years.
As he battled his emotions, Antonelli, who only turned 20 two weeks ago, admitted on team radio that "it feels like a dream".
His win was delivered from the most distant starting position since John Watson raced to victory for McLaren at the 1983 US Grand Prix West in Long Beach from 22nd on the grid.
More pointedly, victory over teammate George Russell opens up a 66-point lead in the title race.
"It’s a dream come true," he said. "What an incredible day. I couldn’t do this without my team, my family and everyone who supports me."
He resisted the temptation, however, to talk about becoming the first Italian world champion since Alberto Ascari in 1953.
"There are still a few races to go, so we will try to keep our heads down. But now, yes, we are going to enjoy today.
"I did not expect this. Unbelievable. Unbelievable. I am so happy. I could not have imagined being here today, but we managed to pull it off, and I am really, really happy."
Antonelli did have one scare in the race, four laps from the end when he was trying to overtake Russell and found himself in the gravel.
"It was quite scary because the tarmac was breaking up, but I still thought I could do the corner.
"I went straight. I was thinking like maybe I lost my chance, but luckily we had the pace and I could bring it home."
Starting Sunday’s race from the back of the grid due to penalties after taking a new power unit, he said he had felt capable of winning after going from 19th to 12th in the opening laps.
Then Charles Leclerc crashed his Ferrari to bring a red-flag stoppage and a restart.
"After the second restart, I was up there, and I knew I could have had a shot for the win. So definitely I believed in it, especially when I was behind George," he said.

"But it was difficult to break away with it all being so strong. At the end we pitted, he stayed out, and he struggled with his tyres at the end, so with fresher tyres we could increase the pace and get the win."
Russell 'disappointed'
His Mercedes teammate Russell was left to rue the moment that his teammate pitted while he remained out on track.
"In hindsight, it's easy to say I should have pitted rather than stayed out," he said.
"I felt like I was holding my own at that point, but I think that's partly why the team wanted us to split strategies.
"I'm disappointed with missing out on the win, but here we are."
Triumphant team boss Toto Wolff had nothing but praise for Antonelli, the first home winner at Monza since Ludovico Scarfiotti in 1966.
"It was unbelievable," he said. "He was so controlled of all race. He kept his head down, took no risks at the start and then, one by one, he passed them. An amazing drive."
Russell added that he was not considering or worrying about the title race.
"We are where we are," he said. "He (Antonelli) has driven incredibly this season. He deserves to lead the championship, and he has a healthy lead.

"I'm not even going to think about the fight or the comeback. I'm just going to every race trying to win it. I'm not putting any pressure on myself in this regard. I just need to try and win more races.
"He is in the best spot and he deserves to be where he is."
dd8b0790fc788983: AT a meeting in a Kuala Lumpur corporate office, the CEO asks, "Any concerns? Nobody speaks. The meeting ends.

In the cafeteria, however there is a roar of activity and discussion among employees, with some openly voicing their views on the problems facing the organisation and what management should do to address them.
Everyone is strident in their views, confidently pontificating on how the lingering problems in the organisation could be resolved.

But all this begs the question as to why there was a deafening silence when the CEO asked if there were any concerns? It is a baffling scenario that can be found in the corporate landscape in Malaysia.

Why is such a scenario prevalent in the Malaysian corporate sector? One reason is the absence of psychological safety- an environment where employees feel able to speak up, ask questions, admit mistakes, challenge ideas and offer suggestions without fear of humiliation or punishment.
This does not mean that an organisation has no accountability. It means people can speak honestly while remaining accountable for their work.
The absence of such an environment can have serious consequences.
Organisations that provide psychological safety for their employees are far more capable of reaching their goals faster and bolstering employee productivity.

Organisations that do not provide such an environment may find that problems remain hidden and decision-makers lack a true sense of what is happening on the ground, as bad news travels slowly upwards.
Managers may therefore have the impression that everything is under control when, in reality, important problems are being kept from them.

The prevailing culture described above depicts what typically takes place where employees say what managers want to hear, which prevents managers from getting a true sense of the problems facing the organisation.
Considering that it would not be beneficial for employees to bring problems to the fore, managers only hear what employees think their bosses want to hear.
In organisations where mistakes are concealed and problems are not discussed, innovation suffers.
It would invariably turn out to be a bureaucratic organisation where employees do not take initiative or responsibility as there are no incentives for doing so.

Decisions become concentrated at the top and are made devoid of the realities of the marketplace. Innovation suffers and employees become less agile in responding to the demands of the marketplace as there is no incentive for them to make decisions.
An organisation that lacks a learning culture and does not inspire confidence among its employees would soon find itself in a tailspin.

Amy Edmondson a reputed Harvard scholar who developed the concept of psychological safety in organisational research said that people perform better when they ask questions, raise concerns, admit mistakes, challenge ideas and ask for help.

Years later, Google conducted a major project entitled "Project Aristotle to understand why some teams performed better than others and the study found that psychological safety was the most important of the five key dynamics associated with effective teams.
Google found that team effectiveness was not simply about putting the smartest or most technically talented people together but how they interacted with each other mattered.

The Google researchers drew on Edmondson's earlier work, demonstrating that the ability of employees to speak up, ask questions and acknowledge mistakes can have a significant bearing on team effectiveness.

There are many examples that Malaysian companies could follow. Pixar is an example of how the creative process depends heavily on people being able to criticise ideas and challenge the work of senior colleagues.
Its Braintrust meetings encourage candid feedback on films in development, allowing creative teams to identify weaknesses before a project reaches the market.
Malaysian managers need to understand that the traditional hierarchical structured organisation would not be able to meet the expectations of customers and markets that are rapidly changing.
To do so, employees must be agile, keep their nose to the grindstone and make decisions swiftly.
If there is no psychological safety, employees would not be willing to take that plunge, leaving the organisation at risk of going downhill in a very short time.

It is therefore important for Malaysian managers to create an environment that inspires confidence among employees to make decisions, take calculated risks and learn from their mistakes without being penalised if organisations here are to navigate a difficult path.
When employees are afraid to speak, silence may give managers the comforting impression that everything is under control.
It may be the clearest warning that something is wrong. An organisation cannot become agile if its people are afraid to speak

d966abaa7fdef6d1: KUALA LUMPUR: The recent corporate earnings of the banking sector shows continuous net interest margins (NIM) squeeze, as the cost of funds increases as banks compete for deposits – a trend that could take off some of the shine of relatively good results.

If the trend continues, banks might have to increase their interest rates, which might cause borrowers to have to pay higher financing costs on their loans, leading to higher costs of doing business and cost of living.

Tradeview Capital fund manager Neoh Jia Man said that the sector witnessed intensified deposit competition as they looked for funds for their loan growth during the quarter under review which led to NIM compression.
"This means banks will increasingly become more selective in extending credit, which would be detrimental to borrowers and could act as a drag on economic growth as a whole," he told Business Times.

Echoing the view, Bank Muamalat Malaysia Bhd chief economist Dr Mohd Afzanizam Abdul Rashid said banks are obliged to observe their liquidity position such as liquidity coverage ratio and net stable funding ratio.
"This will continue to exert competition for deposits especially at a time when depositors, be it individuals or businesses, would require higher deposit rates as means to attract such customers.
"Some banks which have been effective and efficient in managing their cost of funds would be able to offer competitive deposit rates to the customers," he said.

The issue of NIM squeeze is also highlighted by Hong Leong Investment Bank (HLIB) Research in a note on Sept 4, noting that the sector's margins narrowed by two basis points (bps) quarter-on-quarter (QoQ) and three bps year-on-year (YoY).

Declining NIM is pronounced on Alliance Bank Malaysia Bhd, according to data presented by HLIB Research in the note, although the bank remains having the highest figure among the eight banks under the research firm's coverage, at 2.3 per cent.
Five quarters ago, it was at 2.43 per cent.

Affin Bank Bhd had the lowest NIM during the quarter, at 1.5 per cent, followed by RHB Bank Bhd at 1.8 per cent. Malayan Banking Bhd, Public Bank Bhd, CIMB Group Holdings Bhd and Bank Islam Malaysia Bhd chalked 2.1 per cent NIM during the quarter.
Meanwhile, MBSB Research said that NIM weakness is likely to persist, although steep compression is unlikely.
"Most banks don't expect much recovery in subsequent quarters. Expect deposit competition to remain tight, as long as the high loan demand persists," it said.
On the flipside, the firm said it is more confident in the longer-term NIM outlook, when enough higher-yielding loans have been accumulated to bring visible impact to asset yields.
HIGH NIM BANKS OUTPERFORMS

During the second quarter ended June 30, 2026, banks with higher level of NIM outperforms, such as Alliance Bank, which saw its earnings for the quarter – the first quarter for its financial year ending March 31, 2027 – rose 25 per cent to RM248.32 million.
This is despite its revenue only inched up 2.5 per cent during the quarter, to RM630.93 million.

MBSB Research said in a note on Alliance Bank that the bank's management has revised downward its NIM target, from between 2.28 per cent and 2.35 per cent, to between 2.23 per cent and 2.28 per cent, as the bank focuses on growing NII.

"Regardless, management believes that NIMs are already close to bottoming out. The dilution comes largely from growing a lower-yielding loan mix very quickly. NII accretion, not NIM, is the focus," the research firm noted.

MBSB Research maintained its 'Buy' call on Alliance Bank, with a higher target price of RM6.10, compared with RM5.92 prior to the results. The higher target price reflects Alliance Bank's altered earnings prospects, it said.

Meanwhile, CIMB Securities downgraded Affin Bank to 'Hold' with a target price of RM2.30, after the bank announced its second quarter results ended June 30, 2026, which saw core net profit declines 11.13 per cent YoY to RM127.52 million, weighed down by higher impairment allowances and a lower share of profit from associates.

Its NIM compressed by a marginal two bps during the quarter from the preceding quarter, to 1.52 per cent. According to CIMB Research, the bank's management indicated that NIM would have been higher without the delay in the drawdown of a sizeable high-yielding loan.
CIMB Research's downgrade on Affin Bank is premised on its belief that the risk-reward profile of the bank has skewed to the downside, following two consecutive quarters of elevated provisions.

The research firm noted that the next leg of re-rating requires clearer evidence that credit costs have peaked, retail asset quality is stabilising and net credit cost (NCC) is trending back towards normalised levels below 30 bps.
"Accordingly, valuation now requires proof of ROE delivery rather than execution potential alone," states CIMB Research in an August 17 note.
RISKS TO ASSET QUALITY WITH HIGHER LOAN GROWTH
According to Bank Negara Malaysia's July 2026 banking statistics, system loans expanded 5.6 per cent YoY, a slight uptick from 5.5 per cent YoY in June and 5.4 per cent YoY in July 2025.
The expansion was due to stronger expansion in the non-household segment led by electricity, gas, and water alongside transport and communications.
Malacca Securities head of research Loui Low said that small and medium enterprises (SMEs) drove the uptick in loans in the quarter, coupled with working capital, mortgages and corporate activities.
However, Low opined that higher loan growth also comes with a set of risks.
"The main risks are higher funding costs and potential asset-quality pressure if growth becomes too aggressive. But this is unlikely for the near term," he said.
Meanwhile, Afzanizam said that the non-household sector has been posting strong loan growth of 6.4 per cent in July, well above the industry's loan growth of 5.6 per cent during the same period.
This reflects strong investment activities among private firms that are the key catalyst for the loanable funds.
He added that total loans growth for the household sector was steady at 5.0 per cent growth in July, signaling cautious sentiment surrounding the sector.

"At the same time, choices for households for financing have become widely available from the digital platforms including buy now pay later where it caters to a larger crowd with competitive terms such as no interest charge for a few months. This can be a direct competition for credit cards," he said.

Although the street's view is that NIM compression among banks is likely to continue in the second half of the year, Afzanizam said there is a possibility for the overnight policy rate to normalize by 25 bps next year, which could ease pressure on the margins.
"Otherwise, intense competition for deposit will continue to pose a serious challenge on the deposit rates and hence NIM compression," he said.

1cea5e0ef7240cab: KUALA LUMPUR: HHRG Bhd's appointment of Tan Sri Syed Azman Syed Ibrahim as executive chairman puts one of Malaysia's better-known entrepreneurs at the helm of a company that needs more than just a new growth story - it needs stronger earnings.

Syed Azman, the founder of Weststar Group, takes over as HHRG continues to grapple with weaker operating performance while pursuing a diversification strategy beyond its traditional biomass and fibre businesses.
His immediate responsibilities include overseeing the group's 60.7-hectare development in Sungai Petani, Kedah, its Kulim land bank and potential new investment opportunities.

For the nine months ended June 30 2026, HHRG's revenue fell 22.4 per cent year-on-year to RM70.76 million, while it swung to a loss attributable to shareholders of RM5.92 million from a profit of RM2.24 million previously.
The latest quarter was better, with net profit attributable to shareholders of RM643,000, but revenue still fell 23.4 per cent to RM23.3 million.

HHRG attributed the weaker performance to softer furniture demand, the disposal of its mattress manufacturing business, currency movements, shipment delays and weaker biomass sales caused partly by raw-material shortages.
That leaves Syed Azman with a fairly clear challenge: turn HHRG's asset base into recurring, higher-quality earnings.
An industry observer said his experience could be particularly relevant to the Sungai Petani project, which combines industrial and motorsport-related elements.

His background in automotive, commercial vehicles, aviation, property and construction could help HHRG structure partnerships, attract investors and develop commercial components around the site rather than simply monetising the land.
His broader business network could also be useful in bringing strategic partners into projects that HHRG may not have the balance sheet or expertise to develop alone.
But investors may look beyond the appointment itself.
HHRG's shares closed at 14.5 sen on Sept 4, after touching 16 sen earlier in the week.
The stock had risen sharply from 11.5 sen on Aug 26, but remains well below its 52-week high of 18.5 sen.
The market, therefore, appears to be pricing in expectations of change but has yet to see proof.

c006e370fd73177b: KUALA LUMPUR: The investigation into delays in the supply of subsidised fertiliser to padi farmers must determine who was responsible and whether there were weaknesses in the procurement and supply process.
Malaysian Padi Farmers Brotherhood Organisation chairman Abdul Rashid Yob said farmers wanted to know what had happened and who was responsible.
He said farmers had repeatedly raised the fertiliser supply issue with the Agriculture and Food Security Ministry before action was eventually taken.
He added that the investigation should also examine the procurement process, particularly whether decisions made during the evaluation stage were changed when the matter reached the ministry.
"Although there was a procurement board, when the evaluation was carried out there was a merit system, but when it reached the ministry, it changed.
"That is what happened there and we do not know why. So it needs to be investigated properly," he told the New Straits Times.
The issue centres on delays in the supply of Additional Padi Compound Fertiliser 3 (Baja 3) to padi farmers in the Muda Agricultural Development Authority (Mada) area.
The contract of Taveekun Manufacturing Sdn Bhd, which was responsible for supplying Baja 3, was terminated on Aug 27 following the delays.

Agriculture and Food Security Minister Datuk Seri Mohamad Sabu had said Malaysian NPK Fertiliser Sdn Bhd, a subsidiary of Pertubuhan Peladang Kebangsaan, had been appointed to take over the remaining supply to affected farmers.
Delivery of the remaining Baja 3 was to have begun on Sept 3, with the entire process targeted for completion within 10 days.
Mada was also instructed to monitor the deliveries until the fertiliser reached all affected farmers.
When contacted by the NST, Mada said its current focus was on delivering fertiliser to areas that had yet to receive their supplies.
It was reported that 40,000 of the 60,000 padi farmers in the Mada area had yet to receive Baja 3, raising concerns that the delay could affect this season's padi yields.
Rashid said the delays had placed a burden on farmers, who had already spent money preparing their land and managing their crops.
"This failure in management was not caused by weather or other factors. It was a human factor and this is something we deeply regret," he said.
cb88fa29a87e7659: LIVERPOOL: Michael Carrick said Manchester United's start to the Premier League season has not been "that bad" despite conceding twice late on to draw 2-2 at Everton on Sunday.

The Red Devils appeared to have an inviting start against newly-promoted Hull and Ipswich before the trip to the Hill Dickinson Stadium, but have taken just four points from their opening three games.
"It's not that bad," said Carrick. "We've got that close to coming away with three points today, that's football, there are moments we can deal with a bit better, but we'll be fine."
United concentrated their limited transfer budget in reinforcing Carrick's midfield in their three new signings.
But only Youri Tielemans has started the last two games with Andrey Santos dropped to the bench and Carlos Baleba out injured.
The decision not to strengthen an ageing defence could prove costly with United having conceded twice in all three games so far.
Much tougher tests are also to come with Manchester City next up in the league at Old Trafford next weekend.
Twice United looked on course for all three points on Merseyside.
Bryan Mbeumo opened the scoring inside the first minute of the second half and Benjamin Sesko restored the visitors' lead in the 88th minute.
However, they failed to hold out as blistering strikes by Tyrique George and Ainsley Maitland-Niles secured a point for an Everton side short on attacking options.
"Obviously we can't ignore it," added Carrick. "We need to concede less goals to give us a better chance of winning games, but we'll certainly look at that and keep improving.

"I think there's obviously things we need to get better at as a team. There's been two strikes from distance really, two really good strikes from their point of view, that sometimes they fly in the top corner and more often than not they probably don't."
On a more positive note for Carrick has been the form of Marcus Rashford on his return to the club.

The England international's United career appeared over after falling out of favour with Carrick's predecessor Ruben Amorim, which saw him loaned out to Aston Villa and Barcelona in the past two seasons.
"He's done ever so well since he came back. He looked really sharp again today and dangerous," said the United boss.
"That final moment didn't quite drop for him, but nevertheless I thought he created really good opportunities and gave us a big threat throughout the game really."--AFP
53d6fce760190013: LONDON: Xabi Alonso urged Chelsea to use their 2-1 defeat at Arsenal on Sunday as a valuable lesson in the race to catch the Premier League champions.
Blues boss Alonso had presided over free-scoring wins against Fulham and Brighton in the top flight and Luton in the League Cup.
But Arsenal, who have won their opening three games, inevitably proved a far more formidable opponent in a pulsating London derby at the Emirates Stadium.
Morgan Rogers put Chelsea ahead after just 77 seconds, but Kai Havertz equalised in the first half, and Martin Odegaard bagged Arsenal's winner after the interval.
The result once again exposed flaws in Alonso's defence, which has conceded seven goals in three league matches.
Chelsea's vaunted attack was also held in check by Arsenal after Rogers' opener, giving Alonso plenty of food for thought.
"I learnt about the game, about us, about what we are doing, what we are starting," Alonso said.
"This is a process. It's still early days for us. We want to start having clean sheets. They will come.
"The players are committed to working hard, to knowing that we're on the way to compete in each game. Not happy that we couldn't get anything, but we need to keep calm and carry on."
Alonso was beaten for the first time in four games in all competitions since taking charge in the close season.
The Spaniard was frustrated with the way Chelsea failed to take advantage of their early lead.
"It hurts because a defeat has to hurt. It was a very intense game. We had chances to equalise," he said.
"After we scored, there were 15 or 20 minutes where we had to defend too much and we were struggling a bit to get control. Overall, it was a very tight, very intense game.
"We could do better with the second goal. You need to control the overloads on the right side."
'A joy to watch'
While Alonso was annoyed to leave north London empty-handed, he expects Chelsea to be better for the experience.
"The players have this attitude, this desire to compete better game by game to create something we believe in," he said.
"It's game three, and this is going to be a long, long ride."
As Alonso ponders Chelsea's development in the early stages of his rebuild, Arteta finally has the finished article at his disposal after seven years in charge.
The Gunners ended their 22-year run to win the title last season, and lifting that pressure from their shoulders appears to have given them more freedom this season.
"It wasn't the right start but we certainly reacted in an amazing way. I enjoyed the way we competed. We took risks, it was a joy to watch," Arteta said.
"Chelsea have a great coach who can set them up in great condition. We constrained them well. Overall, it was an incredible performance.
"We are very happy, and we need to continue to raise the bar and look to improve every single time. We need to enjoy the victory because it was a big one today."
After an inconsistent season marred by injury last term, Odegaard has been in fine form at the start of the new campaign.
The Norway midfielder has three goals from four games, including the Community Shield, and Arteta said, "I think he is enjoying his football.
"His personal life is settled, he is available, he is training, he has his routine, and if he is intelligent, he can take a lot of benefits from the players around him. He was outstanding today."

247d88f4e5e224fb: NANJIE (China), Sept 7 — The crimson flags on Nanjie village’s “East is Red” Square hang limp in the sweltering summer heat as a trickle of tourists take photos with a towering statue of Chairman Mao Zedong, still gleaming white almost 50 years after he died.
The Great Helmsman, who died September 9 1976, is still very much a fixture in central Henan province’s Nanjie — often dubbed “China’s last Maoist village”.
Nostalgia for Mao’s egalitarian ideals is growing in China as memories of his turbulent rule fade and the country grapples with a slowing economy and inequality.

Mao, who led the 1949 communist revolution against the ruling nationalists, ushered in an era of collectivised ownership he argued would drive industry and unite the country, but his drastic policies are also blamed by historians for mass starvation and millions of deaths.

While the ruling Chinese Communist Party maintains Mao was a revolutionary hero, it publicly acknowledged after his death that his devastating Cultural Revolution was a “grave mistake” — a verdict upheld by subsequent leaders.
In Nanjie, countless murals of the former Chinese leader are plastered around the village.
Residents still live under Maoist principles of shared ownership, while the rest of the country moved on from that economic model.
“I still revere him very much,” Xie Kaiyue, a 22-year-old local university student, said of Mao, who died almost three decades before she was born.
“I think young people in the village and, actually, myself, aren’t as strong-spirited as in the past... People were purer,” she said.

Nearby, electric carts whisked visitors past uniform apartment blocks plastered with socialist slogans as guides explained how cooperative ownership in local enterprises funds free housing for residents.
Party line

Around 500 kilometres (310 miles) north, in the mountain village of Dazhai in Shanxi province, once promoted by Mao as a national model after locals terraformed its arid hills into irrigated fields, tourists reminisce about an era when the Great Helmsman dominated political and social life.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A statue of late Communist leader Mao Zedong on the esplanade of Zhoujiazhuang Commune’s cultural centre in Jinzhou, northern Hebei province, August 18, 2026. — AFP pic
“(People) didn’t have enough to eat or to wear,” Li, a 64-year-old tourist from Xi’an, said of his childhood.
“But... the whole country was full of vigour, and there was a spirit of struggling with heaven, earth, and people to change every aspect of China,” the retiree said.
“Of course I miss it.”
Now, Dazhai is overflowing with shops selling items that support Mao’s personality cult — posters, playing cards, and crockery emblazoned with his image, and the “Little Red Book” of his quotations.
Still, references to dark chapters of his decades in absolute power are tightly censored in public discourse.
The decade-long episode instigated by Mao in 1966 saw intellectuals brutally targeted as “class enemies” and schools shuttered, setting China back for years in education and development.

Private property and land were collectivised, while economic management pushed the country to the Great Famine, which the government says killed around 15 million people, while historians estimate around 20-43 million.
In one museum, text mentioning the Cultural Revolution had been crudely scraped off signage.

“Everything you see in the public domain... is the party line. No one is allowed to deviate from this,” said scholar Xu Chenggang, who was targeted as a child in Beijing during the Cultural Revolution because his father was labelled a “rightist”.
Mao’s face is printed on banknotes, his portrait overlooks Tiananmen Square, and his body is preserved in a mausoleum.
Every year new movies and TV shows dramatising Mao’s life beam the message of his great deeds to public.
Public discussion has been squeezed further under current leader Xi Jinping, who warns against “historical nihilism”, or narratives contradicting the party’s own.
“The Communist Party told people there were mistakes, but what’s the meaning of ‘mistake’? No one knows,” Xu said.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A socialist‑inspired mural at a restaurant in Nanjie Commune, Henan province, August 20, 2026. — AFP pic
‘Great figure’
The sanitised history has left space for romanticised interpretations among youths frustrated by long working hours and intense competition in education and the job market.

In December, a viral video series on Bilibili — a platform popular with those under 30 — argued that the 2017 movie ‘Youth’, which follows young performers in a military dance troupe during the 1970s, was a subtle ode to the Cultural Revolution.
The videos, which praised Mao and blamed capitalist elites for crushing the movement, were removed after gaining over 35 million views in less than a week.

“Today, there is more of a sense that the Cultural Revolution was a period of idealism, where society was fired by ideals and not by the relentless pursuit of money and material goods,” said to Kerry Brown, head of the Lau China Institute in London and author of a recent book on Mao.
“This is, of course, a total fabrication,” he said.
Many also credit Mao with laying the foundation for China to become a modern, technologically advanced nation, said Mobo Gao, professor of Chinese studies at Adelaide University.
“They ask, where did (today’s China) come from? It came from the establishment of the PRC,” said Gao, who lived through the Mao era in rural Jiangxi province.
“Who was the one who really established the PRC? It must be Mao.”
In Shijiazhuang, an industrial city of seven million northeast of Dazhai, 20-year-old Wang Zhihao and his classmates posed with a giant Mao statue opposite the municipal government.
“We admire and revere Chairman Mao very much. He is a great figure,” Wang said, as the sound of elderly residents singing songs praising the Communist Party drifted over from the nearby square.
“He led the founding of New China.” — AFP
6c3f4c4abf5d7140: QAMISHLI (Syria), Sept 7 — At his shop in northeast Syria, Ayaz Ibrahim wiped the dust off bottles of alcohol he said had become too pricey for customers following new regulations from the Islamist authorities.

Residents of the region, which is home to many Kurds, have been feeling the pinch since Damascus took control of the nearby Semalka border crossing with Iraq in April under a deal to integrate Kurdish military and civilian institutions into the state.

Syria’s new Islamist leaders — who toppled longtime ruler Bashar al-Assad in 2024 — have not officially prohibited importing alcohol but have imposed hefty new taxes and stricter rules on its consumption.

As a result, the entry of alcohol via the crossing with Iraqi Kurdistan has become more restricted, “and now only smuggled alcohol reaches us”, said Ibrahim, 30, from the Kurdish-majority city of Qamishli.
“Anything smuggled has a much higher price, plus transport costs... so it’s gone up a lot,” he told AFP.
While Islam prohibits the consumption of alcohol, Syria’s Muslim-majority Kurdish community is considered relatively liberal on the matter, though some still avoid drinking in public.
This year, Syrian media outlets circulated a finance ministry decision to increase taxes on alcoholic beverages, requiring importers and producers to foot the bill.
Finance Minister Mohammed Barnieh later justified the move on social media, saying it aimed to “limit the consumption of products that are damaging to health”.
He added that the measure was also meant to bring in tax revenue for “programmes supporting the health sector and social security”, and to encourage Syrian exports.
But the move has not gone over well with drinkers, according to Ibrahim.
“Our customers are very disgruntled. Before, they would buy half a litre of whisky for US$7, but now it’s US$12,” he told AFP.
“Many of our shelves are now empty” because of a lack of new stock, he said, adding that locally produced alcohol was not an attractive enough alternative for drinkers.
‘It was better before’
“If the situation stays like this, everyone will close their shops because Syrian goods are barely profitable — they aren’t enough to cover the high costs,” Ibrahim said.
At a nearly empty bar in Qamishli, Karl Hussein, 25, said the higher prices “have really affected us”.
“We used to go out every Thursday night and whenever we had the chance, but now we go out once a month.”
Authorities have also stopped people from bringing in alcohol via the airport, one arriving traveller told AFP.
In Qamishli, bar worker Shuaib Hamdi, 28, complained about the lack of business following restrictions from authorities that were “predominantly Islamic in character”.
“These new authorities initially banned the sale of alcoholic beverages in many areas and restricted their sale to specific parts of Damascus and other areas,” he said.
In March, the authorities had limited sales in the capital to a number of Christian districts.
“Apart from our regulars, we might only get one or two other customers a month because of the high prices,” Hamdi said.
Now when he makes cocktails, he said he tries to cut back on some ingredients.
But “this affects the quality of the taste and the service”, he said.
“The customers tell me it was better before.” — AFP
dc7ecd32fed4a762: NEW DELHI, Sept 7 — Indian filmmaker Shaunak Sen’s new documentary began as a “coping” mechanism after a shock cancer diagnosis, but continues the motifs of environmental degradation and caregiving that drove his previous work.

Sen’s All That Breathes, which follows two brothers running a largely self-funded clinic for birds falling victim to Delhi’s polluted air, won top documentary prizes at Sundance and Cannes in 2022 and was nominated for Best Documentary Feature at the 2023 Oscars.

“It became a kind of coping strategy, or a way to deal or dissociate or displace the terror of what you’ve just been told,” Sen, 39, told AFP about his as-yet-untitled project, in an interview from his home in New Delhi.
The diagnosis brought home “the same risks” that make hundreds of birds fall every year from New Delhi’s throat-burning polluted skies — this time on “my own body”, Sen said.

“Whenever you ask most oncologists why this happened, or why this current giant spike in cancer rates is occurring, a lot of them would talk about environmental factors like toxins or chemicals or the air,” he said.

New Delhi and its sprawling metropolitan region of 30 million residents is regularly ranked among the world’s most polluted capitals, due to a mix of emissions from power plants, heavy traffic and the burning of rubbish and crops.
A 2024 study in The Lancet Planetary Health estimated that 3.8 million deaths in India between 2009 and 2019 were linked to air pollution.
‘Meditative’
The central protagonist in Sen’s new work is not the filmmaker himself but his surgeon.
“I did not want to make something that was solipsistically inwards folding,” he said.
It echoes his documentary All That Breathes, where caregiving is at the emotional core of the film.
“What I loved in a surgeon was the ability to completely lose yourself, to be immersed in the absolute present,” he said.
“That feels meditative and contemplative. It’s a kind of melting away of everything extraneous, and you’re in the pinprick of the moment.”
City as ‘wallpaper’
The film is also about Sen’s relationship with New Delhi, where he grew up, went to school and university, and the setting for all his work.
“The city,” he said, is the “wallpaper of this film.”
“In this case, the wallpaper is doing things to me, and I’m kind of reacting to it — through a more personalised lens than I ever have.”
His 2016 debut documentary, Cities of Sleep, examined the city’s homeless population through the lens of sleep, following them in their quest for a safe place to rest.
Sen is also heading to the Toronto International Film Festival in September to screen Termite, his first fiction short, about two Delhi termite exterminators.
Yet the nature of his latest undertaking means it is inevitably different from his previous work.
Sen’s ethnographic approach to filmmaking means shooting characters for long periods to, as he put it, “yield or slow drip certain answers”.
“There’s a deep pleasure in that kind of a thing,” he said.
“Time rewards you with accidents, but in this case, it would be really silly and self-congratulatory for me to say that, ‘I gave this film time.’”
Sen has had surgery, but continues the long road to recovery.

Shooting the film, he said, was a “way to not look directly at a scary thing”, and “to aesthetically convert it into a project, so that you don’t have to stare it in the grim eyes of what it actually is”.
“I guess it’s a kind of a con job.” — AFP
5122b4c7a7f37db0: In the last five years, six youth-led, anti-establishment uprisings have fundamentally reshaped South Asia’s political landscape.

The movements had much in common: they all reflected young people’s aspirations, digital savvy, economic frustrations, and disillusionment with governing elites. But the political systems in which they unfolded process grievances in vastly different ways, leading to sharply divergent outcomes.

The story begins in Myanmar, where the military’s February 2021 overthrow of a democratically elected government triggered popular protests. Unconstrained by concerns about democratic legitimacy, the new regime launched a violent crackdown.

With the peaceful restoration of democracy off the table, a generation of young people had little choice but to form civilian defense forces alongside armed ethnically based organisations. The result was a grinding civil war.

Sri Lanka’s March 2022 Aragalaya movement arose from economic collapse. Dry fuel pumps, prolonged power cuts, and sovereign insolvency destroyed the legitimacy of the Rajapaksa dynasty, which had ruled for the better part of two decades. Protests roiled the island, with demonstrators eventually occupying the presidential palace.

Yet, unlike Myanmar, Sri Lanka did not face surging violence, let alone a prolonged armed conflict. Instead, president Gotabaya Rajapaksa submitted to popular pressure and resigned within the constitutional framework.

In Pakistan, riots erupted in May 2023, following the arrest of former prime minister Imran Khan. This was a case of a populist movement mobilising behind a charismatic leader to challenge the military’s dominance—and it was met with a troop deployment, an internet shutdown, and the dismantling of the opposition’s formal party structures. The “hybrid” regime was preserved, at the cost of persistent political alienation.
Bangladesh’s July 2024 uprising demonstrated how a narrow policy dispute—in this case, student opposition to a skewed quota system for civil-service jobs—can turn into a revolution.
As protests against prime minister Sheikh Hasina’s autocratic regime escalated, Hasina deployed troops to enforce a curfew—with an order to shoot violators on sight.
When the military ultimately refused, Hasina’s hold on power collapsed. She fled the country, opening the way for an interim government to take over.

In Nepal, the September 2025 protests targeted not a single leader, but an oligarchic political class, which had been playing a decade-long game of prime ministerial “musical chairs” while most Nepali youths struggled with soaring unemployment and a lack of opportunity.
For a frustrated Gen Z, a government ban on major social-media platforms was the last straw: using VPNs and alternative apps, Nepal’s youth organised a massive protest.

The authorities attempted to crush it by force, but the protesters fought back, driving the elites out without destroying the parliamentary framework. Nepalis went on to elect a 35-year-old prime minister.
Finally, this summer, India experienced widespread student-led protests, sparked by leaks of university entrance examinations and fuelled by growing anxiety over jobless growth.

Far from threatening the constitutional order, however, the movement confirmed that order’s resilience, as the government offered critical concessions, accepting the education minister’s resignation and proposing administrative and policy reforms with a view towards redirecting protest energy back through established democratic channels.

These six cases show that hyper-connectivity and economic and political alienation are a potent combination. The first fully digitally native generation, Gen Z uses platforms like TikTok, WhatsApp, and Discord to bypass entrenched party structures and orchestrate mass mobilisations.
But that is not all that stands out about Gen Z’s protest style. Unlike their predecessors, today’s protesters are motivated by a sense that they have nothing to lose.

It is not hard to see why: with their economic prospects drastically diminished, despite high educational attainment, what today’s young people see are not flawed institutions in need of reform, but a predatory system robbing them of a viable future.

This imbues their protests with a visceral, existential urgency and makes them resistant to state co-optation. Unimpressed by incremental concessions, they are willing to confront institutional repression head-on.

For all they have in common, these six cases also underscore the difference institutional structures make. In closed regimes that treat power as non-negotiable, such as Myanmar and Pakistan, popular discontent inevitably results in political fragmentation or chronic instability.

In rigid civilian autocracies like Hasina’s Bangladesh, protest is either repressed or revolutionary: the system is unmovable until a single crack—such as the military refusing an order—brings down the whole edifice.
Conversely, systems that allow for political transitions or administrative conciliation can survive generational shocks.

Sri Lanka achieved a peaceful electoral realignment, and Nepal engineered a political reset, which created space for “outsider” political forces. India, for its part, showed how a robust multiparty democracy accommodates discontent before it metastasizes into systemic crisis.

These episodes hold several important lessons. For starters, celebrating aggregate macroeconomic growth but ignoring youth unemployment and systemic corruption is a recipe for instability. Younger generations view economic opportunity as inseparable from political accountability—and they will, sooner or later, demand both.

Moreover, military-dominated governance is poorly suited for this era of hyper-connectivity. While crackdowns and coercion can suppress dissent temporarily, they destroy state legitimacy over time. Relying on them risks prolonged civil disorder.

Finally, dismantling systemic corruption is only the first step. Durable institutions, with democratic pressure valves and credible mechanisms for addressing young people’s aspirations, are also essential.
That is why India’s recent uprising reaffirmed its democracy, while Nepal and Sri Lanka, as well as Bangladesh, have faced considerable post-uprising instability.

The Arab Spring revolutions a decade and a half ago ultimately ended in military counter-revolution, autocratic revival, or institutional paralysis, owing to absent or fragile democratic legacies and ideological hijacking. But many South Asian societies possess deep parliamentary traditions, vibrant civil societies, and functional constitutional mechanisms.

If South Asian countries can harness young people’s activist energy to deliver effective, responsive governance and job-creating reforms, they will put themselves on a path towards a brighter, more resilient, and more prosperous future. And they will become a model for how the Global South can align demographic weight with democratic accountability.

Shashi Tharoor, a former UN under-secretary-general and former Indian minister of state for external affairs and minister of state for human resource development, is a fourth-term elected member of Parliament for the opposition Indian National Congress.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
aa32e682f5442e62: Malaysia kini mahu bergerak lebih jauh daripada sekadar menjadi lokasi pengeluaran dunia. Dalam prabelanjawan 2027, kerajaan menekankan aspirasi "Made by Malaysia" supaya lebih banyak produk, teknologi dan harta intelek direka, dibangunkan dan dimiliki rakyat Malaysia. Semikonduktor, kecerdasan buatan (AI), ekonomi digital dan peralihan tenaga pula terus diletakkan sebagai sektor strategik negara.

Angkanya memang memberangsangkan. Malaysia merekodkan RM218.5 bilion pelaburan diluluskan bagi separuh pertama 2026, dengan hampir 100,000 pekerjaan dijangka diwujudkan. Tetapi, bagi sebuah negara yang mahu melonjak ke tahap ekonomi bernilai tinggi, persoalan utamanya bukan lagi sekadar berapa banyak pelaburan yang masuk. Lebih penting ialah berapa banyak keupayaan, teknologi dan nilai yang akhirnya benar-benar menjadi milik kita.

Untuk itu kita tidak kekurangan dasar. Kita juga tidak kekurangan universiti, penyelidik, jurutera atau bakat. Persoalan lebih sukar ialah: mengapa begitu banyak ilmu, penyelidikan dan perancangan kita masih mengambil masa terlalu lama untuk menjadi teknologi, produk, penyelesaian dan kekuatan ekonomi? Soalan itu kembali bermain di fikiran saya selepas menghadiri The 2nd China-Southeast Asia Kerry Youth Scientist Forum bertemakan "China-Southeast Asia: Industrial Trade, Green Development and Common Prosperity in a Changing Global Landscape" di Nanjing baru-baru ini.

Setiap kali menghadiri persidangan di China, saya tertarik bukan semata-mata pada apa yang dibincangkan, tetapi bagaimana sarjananya menghubungkan ilmu dengan persoalan besar negara. Mereka boleh membincangkan perdagangan, teknologi, pembangunan hijau dan kemakmuran bersama dalam satu kerangka jelas, iaitu ilmu mesti akhirnya melahirkan keupayaan untuk bertindak.

China tentunya bukan model yang perlu kita salin bulat-bulat. Sistem politik, sejarah dan skala negaranya sangat berbeza. Tetapi, ada sesuatu yang wajar dipelajari, iaitu bagaimana sebuah negara mengambil ilmu dari mana-mana tanpa kehilangan pasak sendiri.

Dalam satu perbualan semasa menghadiri persidangan tersebut, seorang rakan memberitahu mereka mengadaptasi pendekatan tamadun Barat ke dalam acuan tamadun mereka sendiri. Ia mengingatkan saya kepada gagasan lama 中体西用 (zhōng tǐ xī yòng) yang bermaksud "pembelajaran China sebagai teras, pembelajaran Barat sebagai gunaan". Mudahnya, ambil teknologi, kaedah dan kepakaran terbaik dari luar, tetapi jangan serahkan kepada orang lain hak menentukan untuk apa semuanya digunakan.
China belajar dari Barat tanpa perlu menjadi Barat

Di sinilah bezanya antara meminjam alat dengan meminjam arah. Pelajaran kedua lebih dekat dengan cabaran Malaysia hari ini di mana China sangat serius memendekkan jarak antara mengetahui dengan melaksanakan. Ilmu yang ditimba terus dimajukan dan diterjemahkan kepada teknologi atau dasar, kemudian dibiayai, diuji, dikembangkan dan dinilai semula. Penyelidikan tidak dianggap selesai apabila makalah diterbitkan. Nilainya diuji apabila ia masuk ke kilang, pasaran, komuniti atau sistem pentadbiran. Inilah formula dan model kitaran serta rantaian ilmu mereka yang seharusnya menjadi amalan di Malaysia juga.

Dalam tradisi pemikiran China, ada konsep 知行合一 (zhī xíng hé yī), kesatuan antara pengetahuan dengan tindakan. Ilmu yang tidak diterjemahkan kepada tindakan belum dianggap lengkap. Hari ini, falsafah lama itu seolah-olah memperoleh nafas baharu dalam bentuk moden melalui hubungan lebih rapat antara universiti, kerajaan, industri, pembiayaan dan pelaksanaan. Kita dapat melihat hasilnya dalam pelbagai bidang seperti usaha mereka dalam pembasmian kemiskinan kepada kereta elektrik, panel solar, bateri, infrastruktur dan kini AI.
China sendiri masih berdepan banyak masalah: tekanan demografi, hutang, ketidakseimbangan ekonomi, persaingan geopolitik dan persoalan kebebasan. Jadi, ini bukan tulisan untuk meromantiskan China.
Fokus pelaksanaan dan impak

Contoh kejayaan paling besar kitaran ilmu mereka agenda ialah pembasmian kemiskinan China. Dalam tempoh sekitar empat dekad, China berjaya mengeluarkan kira-kira 800 juta rakyat daripada kemiskinan tegar — satu skala transformasi sosial yang sukar ditandingi. Pada 2021, China mengisytiharkan kemiskinan mutlak di kawasan luar bandar telah dihapuskan. Sudah tentu angka, ukuran dan pendekatan China boleh diperdebatkan. Tetapi, perkara yang lebih penting ialah keupayaan menterjemahkan pengetahuan kepada tindakan pada skala sangat besar. Dasar pembasmian kemiskinan tidak berhenti pada sasaran nasional. Keluarga miskin dikenal pasti secara terperinci, keadaan setempat dipetakan dan bentuk intervensi disesuaikan dengan keperluan masing-masing.

Inilah yang saya maksudkan dengan melengkapkan rantaian ilmu dan amal. Pengetahuan menghasilkan dasar; dasar diterjemahkan kepada program; program dilaksanakan hingga ke lapangan; hasilnya dinilai dan diperbaiki. Malaysia sebenarnya tidak bermula dari kosong. Kita mempunyai universiti yang baik, penyelidik, jurutera, ekosistem elektrik dan elektronik matang, industri semikonduktor berdekad lamanya serta pelbagai dana inovasi. Kita juga mahu bergerak daripada kekuatan tradisional dalam pemasangan, pembungkusan dan pengujian semikonduktor kepada kegiatan bernilai lebih tinggi seperti reka bentuk cip, pembungkusan termaju dan R&D. Tetapi, cita-cita untuk menaikkan rantaian nilai tidak akan berlaku hanya dengan menambah satu lagi pelan induk. Kita perlu bertanya beberapa soalan kurang selesa. Berapa banyak penyelidikan universiti benar-benar mengubah dasar? Berapa banyak paten menjadi syarikat atau produk? Berapa banyak dana R&D akhirnya menghasilkan penyelesaian yang digunakan secara meluas? Berapa pantas idea baik dapat bergerak merentas birokrasi, universiti, industri dan pembiayaan?

Masalah Malaysia mungkin bukan kekurangan ‘aql (idea dan sebagainya). Masalahnya ialah rantaian daripada ‘aql kepada amal (strategi, dasar, program dan sebagainya) yang sering terputus di tengah jalan. Kita mempunyai ilmu, tetapi mekanisme yang menghubungkan ilmu dengan tindakan belum cukup tangkas. Sebab itu aspirasi "Made by Malaysia" tidak boleh menjadi sekadar slogan baharu untuk menggantikan slogan lama. Ia menuntut perubahan pada keseluruhan ekosistem, di mana cara universiti menilai penyelidikan, cara kerajaan membiayai inovasi, cara industri bekerjasama dengan akademia, cara perolehan awam memberi ruang kepada teknologi tempatan, dan sejauh mana birokrasi bersedia mengambil risiko terhadap idea baharu.
Nilai dan kompas pembangunan Malaysia

Namun, ada satu lagi pelajaran China yang lebih besar. Kemajuan bukan hanya soal seberapa pantas kita menguasai teknologi, tetapi nilai apa yang menentukan arah penggunaannya. China mempunyai ti, yakni teras yang membolehkan ilmu luar ditafsir dalam kerangka sejarah dan tamadunnya sendiri. Dalam pembangunan hijau misalnya, gagasan moden tentang kelestarian turut dihubungkan dengan idea lama tentang keharmonian manusia dan alam.

Malaysia juga perlu bertanya apakah ti kita? Jika AI, teknologi hijau, ekonomi digital dan model pembangunan semuanya kita import, adakah kita turut mengimport sekali ukuran tentang apa yang dianggap sebagai kemajuan? Dalam khazanah Malaysia, khususnya tradisi Melayu-Islam, kita sudah mempunyai bahasa yang kaya, antaranya tawhid, adab, amanah, kesejahteraan dan sejahtera. Tetapi konsep-konsep ini tidak cukup jika hanya muncul dalam ucapan, slogan atau dokumen rasmi. Ia mesti menjadi prinsip yang mempengaruhi bagaimana teknologi dibangunkan, bagaimana kekayaan diagihkan dan bagaimana kemajuan dinilai. Teknologi sangat cekap belum tentu membawa masyarakat ke arah yang betul.

Sebab itu soalan "adakah ia berkesan?" mesti sentiasa disertai dua lagi soalan — berkesan untuk siapa, dan menuju ke mana? Malaysia tidak perlu menjadi China. Malah, kita tidak seharusnya cuba. Tetapi, dalam usaha bergerak daripada "Made in Malaysia" kepada "Made by Malaysia", ada satu sikap yang wajar kita pelajari, iaitu keberanian mengambil ilmu terbaik dari mana sahaja, keupayaan menukarnya dengan pantas kepada tindakan, dan keyakinan untuk menambat kemajuan pada pasak sendiri.
China sudah lama mencari dan kini menemui bentuknya. Persoalannya sekarang — apakah bentuk Malaysia? Apatah lagi bila kita juga masih bergelut mentafsirkan apakah identiti Bangsa Malaysia.
Penulis ialah profesor di Jabatan Sains Politik dan Pengajian Madani Universiti Islam Antarabangsa Malaysia serta Felo Sejahtera, RCE Tongyeong Sejahtera Forest, Korea Selatan.
